summary.text:
Three things stand out. The deposits first: £14.6m of a £57.1m portfolio lent to four other councils at 6.00% to 7.00% for between 28 and 33 days — £5m each to Bexley and Newham at 7.00% — against money market funds in the same portfolio paying 3.75% to 3.84%. A 320 basis point spread for a month's money, and it is what turned a £0.552m income budget into £2.534m.

Second, the £55m drawn in the final quarter: ten-year EIP at 4.83%, which appears in our PWLB file as loan 911338 on exactly those terms. Paragraph 4.2 names the reason — capital programme spend and "the ongoing impact of financing the DSG deficit".

Third, a £1m loan at 10.25% maturing 2044 whose premium alone is roughly £548,000 today, over half the principal again. The most extreme single legacy coupon in the library so far.

Note carefully: they quote internal borrowing against long-term borrowing excluding PFI (£145.7m). On the full identity, against gross debt of £231.160m, it is £99.650m. Both are right on their own definition and any quotation must say which.

Blocked — the appendix names no officer at all.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on Appendix C, the treasury report that went to Cabinet on 21 May. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and this one came out cleaner than most. Paragraph 4.3 describes a new long-term loan of £55.0m taken in the final quarter on a ten-year repayment term at 4.83%. In our PWLB file that is loan 911338 — EIP profile, £55,000,000, 4.83%, maturing 10 March 2036. Principal, rate, term and repayment profile all match, which tells us we're looking at the same book. Across all 28 loans we hold £173.1m at a weighted 4.432%, sitting inside the £185.1m of long-term borrowing you report. Your PI3 also ties: gross debt £231.160m over a CFR of £330.810m is 69.88%, against the 70% in the table.

One point of care on our side rather than yours. Paragraph 4.3 compares the CFR to long-term borrowing excluding PFI, giving about £145.7m of internal borrowing. On the full identity — CFR less gross external debt of £231.160m — it is £99.650m. Both are right on their own definition, and we mention it only because the two get quoted interchangeably elsewhere and they are eleven figures apart.

Now the part that made us look twice, which is Table 1. £14.6m of a £57.1m portfolio was out with four other councils — £5m each to Bexley and Newham at 7.00% for 32 days, £4.6m to Uttlesford at 6.15% for 28 days, £2m to Surrey at 6.00% for 33 days. In the same table your money market funds are paying 3.75% to 3.84% and the NatWest instant access account 1.75%. That is a spread of well over three points for a month's money, and it is visibly what turned a £0.552m income budget into £2.534m.

We track inter-authority pricing across the sector precisely because it is invisible from any one council's papers — nobody publishes what everyone else is paying, so the only way to know whether 7.00% was the going rate that week or an outlier is to see the whole market. Alongside it our monthly PWLB breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows the borrowing side: July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. Thin borrowing markets and rich deposit rates tend to arrive together, and both are in the same picture.

Two smaller observations. First, the £55m: paragraph 4.2 gives the reason as capital programme spend "and the ongoing impact of financing the DSG deficit". Borrowing at ten years to carry a schools deficit against a statutory override that currently runs to March 2028 is a specific position, and we mention it only because we hold the same fact pattern for a number of authorities now and it is going to become a sector conversation rather than a local one.

Second, and this is a curiosity more than anything: you hold £1m at 10.25% maturing in 2044. On today's curve its premium alone is roughly £548,000 — over half the principal again, and the most extreme single legacy coupon we've come across. There is nothing to be done about it and we are not suggesting there is. Across the whole book you sit at about £10.3m of net discount on a £172.4m balance, which is a mild position by current standards. That is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis; ours is indicative, the DMO's is the only binding quote, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment.

On training, four fit Herefordshire. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go directly to Table 1. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator and PWLB repayment structures cover the EIP question that the £55m raises. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
